prompt: `early.go` starts a goroutine that prints a greeting, then `main` prints its own line and returns. In five runs the greeting never appeared. Why?
hint: What happens to every goroutine when `main` returns?

choices.text: The `go` statement delays a goroutine until `main` blocks
choices.why: A goroutine is ready to run the moment it is created. Nothing guarantees it gets a processor before `main` returns, and nothing guarantees it does not.

choices.text: Returning from `main` ends the process, goroutines and all
choices.why: Right. The goroutine had not been given a processor yet, and nothing asked anybody to wait for it.

choices.text: `fmt.Println` cannot be called from a goroutine
choices.why: `waited.go` calls the same function from a goroutine and printed it five times.

choices.text: The output of a goroutine goes to standard error, which the loop did not show
choices.why: A goroutine writes wherever its code writes. `Println` writes to standard output whoever calls it.

prompt: Someone fixes `early.go` by adding `time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond)` at the end of `main`. The greeting now appears on their machine. What is wrong with the fix?
hint: Is the order now promised, or only likely?

choices.text: Nothing: 100 ms is longer than any goroutine needs to start
choices.why: Usually long enough is not the same as promised. A loaded machine can take longer, and the program says nothing about what it is waiting for.

choices.text: It is a guess about timing, where `wg.Wait` would be a promise
choices.why: Right. `wg.Wait` returns only after the goroutine has, on every machine and every run.

choices.text: `time.Sleep` blocks every goroutine, so the greeting cannot print
choices.why: A sleep blocks only the goroutine that calls it. Lesson 1's `wait.go` overlapped four of them.

choices.text: The sleep makes the program use a second processor
choices.why: Sleeping needs no processor at all; it changes timing, not parallelism.

prompt: A goroutine started with `wg.Go` writes to a nil map and panics. `main` has a `defer` that prints a line. What does the run show?

choices.text: The deferred line, then the panic, because `main` unwinds first
choices.why: The deferred call belongs to `main`'s goroutine, and the panic happened in another one. The process ended under `main` without running it.

choices.text: Nothing: `wg.Go` recovers the panic and the program goes on
choices.why: `wg.Go` recovers it only to raise it again, which is the `[recovered, repanicked]` note in the trace.

choices.text: A panic trace and exit status 2, with no deferred line
choices.why: Right. A panic in any goroutine ends the whole program, and `main`'s defer never runs.

choices.text: `main is done`, because `wg.Wait` returns when a goroutine fails
choices.why: `wg.Wait` never returned: the process was gone before it could.

prompt: In a panic trace, the line `created by sync.(*WaitGroup).Go in goroutine 1` says the failing goroutine was started from goroutine number ___, which is `main`.
hint: The number at the end of that line.

prompt: `x := 1; go show(x); x = 2` — the goroutine runs a moment after `x = 2`. What does `show` receive?
hint: When are the arguments of a `go` statement evaluated?

choices.why: Right. The arguments are evaluated by the goroutine running the `go` statement, at that moment, and copied.

choices.text: 2, because the goroutine reads `x` when it starts running
choices.why: That is what a closure reading `x` would do. A call's arguments were already copied when the statement ran.

choices.text: Either 1 or 2, depending on the scheduler
choices.why: There is no race here: the value was copied before the goroutine existed.

choices.text: A compile error, since `x` is changed after `go`
choices.why: Nothing forbids changing a variable after passing its value to a call.

prompt: `many.go` reported `per goroutine: 2048 bytes` of stack. How many kilobytes is that?
`ulimit -s` printed `8192` and a goroutine started with 2048 bytes. Why does the lesson say a thread costs more than its raw size suggests?
hint: Two differences: when the stack is reserved, and what creating one involves.

choices.text: Threads use 8192 bytes, four times a goroutine
choices.why: `ulimit -s` reports kilobytes: 8192 KiB is 8 MiB, four thousand times a goroutine's start.

choices.text: Its 8 MiB stack is reserved up front, and each one is a system call
choices.why: Right. A goroutine's stack starts at two kilobytes, grows only when needed, and starting one never leaves the process.

choices.text: A thread's stack can never grow, so it is sized for the worst case
choices.why: The section's point is the reservation and the system call, not a rule about growth.

choices.text: The kernel copies every thread's stack on each switch
choices.why: No copying happens on a switch. The runtime copies a goroutine's stack only when it grows.

prompt: `many.go` printed `goroutines: 100001` while the goroutines waited, and `after they return: 1`. What is the extra one in 100001?
hint: Which goroutine was alive before the loop and after it?

choices.text: The goroutine that closes `release`
choices.why: `main` closes it itself; no separate goroutine does.

choices.text: The garbage collector, counted as a goroutine
choices.why: `NumGoroutine` left it out: after they returned the count was 1, and that one is `main`.

choices.text: `main`
choices.why: Right. `main` runs in a goroutine of its own, the one still alive at the end.

choices.text: An off-by-one in `wg.Go`
choices.why: `wg.Go` started exactly one goroutine per call. The extra is the one that called it.

prompt: A server holds one goroutine per open connection. Under load it uses 3 GB and keeps 40,000 goroutines. Going by section 03, where does most of the memory go?
hint: 40,000 times two kilobytes is about 80 MB.

choices.text: Into the goroutines' starting stacks, two kilobytes each
choices.why: Those come to about 80 MB, a small part of 3 GB.

choices.text: Into what the goroutines hold: buffers, connections and their data
choices.why: Right. The goroutine itself is the floor; a real one holds what it works on, and that fills memory.

choices.text: Into 40,000 operating-system threads
choices.why: Goroutines are placed on a few threads, about as many as `GOMAXPROCS` plus a spare or two.

choices.text: Into the scheduler's run queues
choices.why: A queue holds references to goroutines, not copies of them, and costs next to nothing.

prompt: Match each of the scheduler's letters with what it stands for.
hint: One is code, one is an operating-system thing, one is a licence.

pairs.right: a goroutine: its stack and where it had got to
a licence to run Go code, `GOMAXPROCS` of them

right_distractors: a lock that protects shared memory

prompt: At 505ms the trace showed `runqueue=2` and local queues `[ 1 0 0 1 ]`, with all four Ps busy. How many goroutines of `busy.go` were waiting rather than running?
hint: The global queue plus every local queue.

prompt: A P's local run queue is empty while another P has a backlog. What does the scheduler do?
hint: Section 03 names the move with a verb from crime.

choices.text: It leaves the idle P waiting until `main` hands it work
choices.why: `main` does not distribute goroutines; the scheduler does, on its own.

choices.text: It starts another thread for each waiting goroutine
choices.why: Threads stay few. Eight goroutines ran on five threads.

choices.text: The idle P steals half of the other's queue
choices.why: Right, after looking at the global queue. Work stealing keeps every processor busy while there is work.

choices.text: It raises `GOMAXPROCS` to match the backlog
choices.why: `GOMAXPROCS` is fixed for the run unless the program changes it. The trace said 4 throughout.

prompt: A goroutine makes a system call that blocks for two seconds. `GOMAXPROCS` is 4 and three other goroutines are ready. What happens to its P?
hint: The thread is stuck in the kernel; the licence does not have to be.

choices.text: It is stuck with the thread, leaving three Ps for the ready goroutines
choices.why: The runtime does not let a blocked thread hold a licence it cannot use.

choices.text: It is handed to another thread, so all four Ps keep running Go code
choices.why: Right. That handover is why a Go program has a few more threads than processors.

choices.text: The whole program pauses until the call returns
choices.why: Only that goroutine and its thread wait. The others carry on.

choices.text: The goroutine is preempted by a signal and its call cancelled
choices.why: Preemption interrupts Go code that runs too long; it does not cancel a system call.

prompt: `hog.go` loops with `for {}` on one processor. With default settings `main` still printed; with `GODEBUG=asyncpreemptoff=1` the program hung. What did that setting remove?
hint: Since Go 1.14 the runtime interrupts a long-running goroutine in a particular way.

choices.text: The second processor `main` was running on
choices.why: `hog.go` set `GOMAXPROCS` to 1 itself, in both runs.

choices.text: The timer that wakes `main` from its sleep
choices.why: The timer fired; `main` simply never got the processor back to act on it.

choices.text: Preemption by signal, leaving only the kind at a function call
choices.why: Right. The loop calls no function, so nothing could take the processor back.

choices.text: The garbage collector's pauses
choices.why: The setting is about preemption; the collector has nothing to do with this hang.

prompt: `timeout` stopped the hung `hog` after three seconds, and the shell reported its exit status as ___.
hint: The last line of the `hog` transcript.

prompt: Order these by how much each one starts with, smallest first.
hint: A goroutine's stack, a thread's stack, and what a hundred thousand goroutines took.
items: a hundred thousand goroutines' stacks, 195 MiB

prompt: A program starts a goroutine per file to hash 10,000 files, then `main` prints "all hashed" and returns. Some runs print fewer hashes than files. Which change fixes it for every run?

choices.text: Lower the count to 1,000 goroutines at a time
choices.why: The cost of goroutines is not the problem; `main` returning before they finish is.

choices.text: Set `GOMAXPROCS` to the number of files
choices.why: More parallelism makes them faster, and still leaves `main` free to return first.

choices.text: Start them with `wg.Go` and call `wg.Wait` before printing
choices.why: Right. `wg.Wait` returns only after every goroutine has, which is a promise rather than a timing.

choices.text: Sleep one second per thousand files before printing
choices.why: A sleep long enough on this machine is a guess about the next one.
